summary: Updates the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries. It deals with the definition of a "global" prefix and fixes several errors in registry entries. It updates RFC 6890 and is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: There is a list of special internet addresses with unusual rules. This fixes mistakes in the list and clears up a word.

questions: ipv4 ipv6 special use addresses update
what is a unique local address
subtitle: Fixes and clarifications to IP address registries for special-purpose addresses.

tldr.problem: RFC 6890 documented special-purpose IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges but defined the term "global" in a misleading way that conflated allocation scope with routing reachability. Additionally, several registry entries contained errors.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC replaces the ambiguous term "global" with "globally reachable" to clarify whether addresses can be forwarded beyond administrative boundaries. It also corrects errors in specific registry entries for IPv4 and IPv6 special-purpose addresses, such as the limited broadcast prefix and several IPv6 ranges.
tldr.outcome: The IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries are now more clearly documented, with removed ambiguity about what "global" means and corrections to registry entries to ensure data integrity.

today: RFC 8190 updates RFC 6890. The IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries have been updated with the clearer "globally reachable" terminology and corrections. This is best current practice for anyone consulting or maintaining these registries.

sections.title: What Are Special-Purpose Addresses
sections.content:
The IETF occasionally reserves specific IP address blocks for special purposes. For example, the IPv4 block 0.0.0.0/8 (as defined in RFC 1122) represents the local or "this" network, and the IPv6 block fe80::/10 (as defined in RFC 4291) is reserved for link-local unicast addresses.

These special-purpose addresses have unique forwarding rules and are documented in IANA registries. RFC 6890 documented the IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries and listed which addresses could be forwarded globally. However, the definition of "global" in RFC 6890 was misleading because it did not clearly distinguish between allocation scope (whether the address space is allocated globally) and routing/reachability scope (whether packets with those addresses can be forwarded beyond administrative domain boundaries).
sections.eli5: The internet has special addresses with unusual rules, like 127.0.0.1 which means your own computer. There is a list that says which special addresses are allowed on the regular internet and which are not. But the words used were confusing.

sections.title: The Problem with "Global"
sections.content:
RFC 6890 defined the term "global" without accounting for its multiple meanings in networking. Specifically, an IP address can be global in two different ways:

Global allocation scope: The address block is allocated at the global level by IANA, meaning it is recognized throughout the Internet as reserved for a specific purpose.

Global reachability: An IP datagram with a destination address from that block can be forwarded beyond the boundaries of a single administrative domain (such as a local network or organization).

RFC 6890's definition mixed these concepts, creating confusion about which special-purpose addresses could legitimately be routed across the public Internet. This RFC clarifies by replacing all instances of "global" with "globally reachable", defined as a boolean value indicating whether datagrams to that address can be forwarded beyond an administrative domain.
sections.eli5: "Global" is a confusing word. It could mean the address was given out by the world's governing body, or it could mean the address works on the whole internet. This fixes it by using a clearer word: "globally reachable" means whether it can be sent across the internet.

sections.title: Registry Structure and Relationships
sections.content:
Both the IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries include columns for "Destination" (whether the address block is suitable as a destination address), "Forwardable" (whether it may be forwarded), and the newly-clarified "Globally Reachable" (whether it can be forwarded beyond administrative boundaries).

RFC 6890 established a relationship between these fields: if "Destination" is FALSE, then both "Forwardable" and "Globally Reachable" must also be FALSE. This same relationship is preserved in RFC 8190. The change affects only the terminology and a few specific registry entries where errors existed or ambiguity needed clarification.
sections.eli5: Each special address has three yes/no properties: can you send it as a destination, can you forward it, and can you send it far away. If one of them is no, the others must be no too. The registries now use clearer words for these.

sections.title: IPv4 Registry Updates
sections.content:
The primary IPv4 registry change affects the limited broadcast prefix (255.255.255.255/32). RFC 8190 updates the "Reserved-by-Protocol" flag for this address from FALSE to TRUE, aligning the registry with the reservation of the limited broadcast address documented in Section 7 of RFC 919.

The limited broadcast address is used by hosts to send datagrams to all hosts on the local network segment without knowing the network's broadcast address. It is reserved and handled specially by all IP implementations, so marking it as "Reserved-by-Protocol" more accurately reflects its nature.
sections.eli5: The address 255.255.255.255 is special because it sends a message to everyone on your local network. The registry now correctly marks it as reserved by the protocol.

sections.title: IPv6 Registry Updates
sections.content:
Several IPv6 special-purpose address blocks required updates to the registry:

TEREDO prefix (2001::/32): The "Globally Reachable" value changed from FALSE to "N/A [2]", with a new footnote referencing RFC 4380. TEREDO is a mechanism for tunneling IPv6 over UDP through Network Address Translations (NATs), and its reachability is context-dependent.

Unique-Local addresses (fc00::/7): The "Globally Reachable" value changed from FALSE to "False [7]", with a footnote explaining that while Unique-Local addresses are drawn from the IPv6 Global Unicast Address range, they are specifically designed not to be globally routed. This clarifies that they have global allocation scope but not global reachability.

EID Space for LISP (2001:5::/32) and 6to4 (2002::/16): Both entries required footnote renumbering to accommodate the new entries but did not have substantive changes to their registry properties.
sections.eli5: Several special IPv6 addresses needed fixes: one (TEREDO) changed because its reachability depends on context, and one (Unique-Local) changed to clarify that it is globally allocated but locally used, like a private office phone number.

sections.title: Impact and Best Current Practice
sections.content:
RFC 8190 is published as a Best Current Practice (BCP), making it guidance for operators and implementers rather than a mandatory standard. The clarifications help ensure that anyone consulting the IANA Special-Purpose Address Registries understands which addresses can be routed across the public Internet and which are restricted to specific contexts.

This RFC updates RFC 6890 but does not change the fundamental properties of the special-purpose addresses themselves. Implementations that already handle these addresses correctly will continue to work. The changes primarily benefit documentation, registry maintenance, and clarity for operators maintaining routing policies and firewall rules.
sections.eli5: This is guidance (not a requirement) for people who manage networks. It does not break anything that already works, but it makes the rules clearer and more accurate.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
RFC 8190 notes that it does not raise any security issues beyond those discussed in RFC 6890. The clarifications about which addresses are "globally reachable" help with security policy: administrators who want to prevent certain traffic from leaving their networks can use the registry to identify which address ranges should be blocked at border routers.

For example, Unique-Local addresses (fc00::/7) are now explicitly noted as not globally routed, which helps security administrators understand that filtering them at a border router is appropriate. Conversely, understanding that TEREDO reachability is context-dependent helps with understanding tunnel endpoints and potential security implications.
sections.eli5: The clearer rules help network administrators write better rules about which internet addresses to block or allow, making networks safer.
